claims.text: Mesh stops replaying history on arrival: web/src/hooks/useSharedEvents.tsx connects with no cursor on every page load, and internal/api/events.go's handleStreamEvents treats an absent Last-Event-ID/from as 'from the beginning of this namespace's event log', admitting every historical run.created/run.completed lifecycle event; routes/Mesh.tsx turns each into a run-added placeholder then a 3.4s linger-and-remove, so the whole run history animates through the mesh at speed. The fix is a server-side tail-only connect, ordered stream-first so the two reads have a defined boundary: the Mesh opens the stream in an explicit tail-only mode, the server's first frame is a snapshot marker naming the event-log high-water mark it will stream after, and only then does the Mesh load active runs from GET /runs, buffering every streamed event until that response lands and applying it on top keyed by run id. Reading the marker before the snapshot query makes that boundary at-least-once rather than at-most-once, which is what the data allows: GET /runs returns a pagination cursor over runs and can never carry the event log's ULID high-water mark, so no single call can hand back both atomically, and a transition committed between the two reads must therefore appear in both and reconcile, never fall between them. A Go change plus a client cursor-and-reconcile rule.

honesty_conditions.text: A fresh EventSource connect admits only events with an id after the server's snapshot cursor; a server test seeds terminal runs and asserts none of their lifecycle events are streamed on a cursor-less connect, and the Mesh e2e asserts mesh.events_total == 0 after load with no new activity.

No run transition falls between the two reads: a run.created committed after the stream's snapshot marker but before GET /runs returns is present in the reconciled Mesh state exactly once, asserted by a test that interleaves the two, and the marker's id is read from the same events table the stream then advances through, so the boundary is one cursor and not two clocks.

claims.instruction: Go: add an explicit tail-only mode to handleStreamEvents (?from=latest) whose first frame is a snapshot marker (event: stream.snapshot) carrying the events table's current max id for the namespace, then stream strictly after that id; the cursor-less default is left as it is. Client: Mesh connects with ?from=latest, waits for the marker, then loads GET /runs; every event that arrives before that response resolves is buffered and applied after the snapshot, idempotently by run id, so a run present in both is added once. Tests: internal/api/events_test.go seeds terminal runs and asserts the marker id and that no event at or before it is streamed; one test commits a run.created between the marker and the snapshot read and asserts the reconciled state holds that run exactly once; web e2e asserts mesh.events_total after load.

claims.text: The mesh is a star by construction, not by data: web/src/domain/mesh.ts assembleMeshGraph emits only actor→control-plane and run→actor edges and layoutMesh puts actors on a ring around the center, so the picture carries no relationship between actors. The records already hold more: Actor rows carry kind, protocol, capabilities and metadata (web/src/api/types.ts) — the capabilities document holding the host block each bridge measured about itself, hostname included — node-run rows carry run_id, node_id and actor_id, and published workflow IRs name which actor each node — enough to draw actor↔machine from that reported hostname, actor↔workflow-node, run↔workflow and capability groupings instead of spokes. The endpoint_ref column those rows also carry is NOT that host fact: it is nullable caller-supplied address text, one stale copy per superseded revision, dropped by migrations/pending/0036 after the dial-in cutover and absent entirely on a dial-in bridge.

claims.text: The mesh node style the operator likes is web/src/components/MeshCanvas.tsx: Canvas-2D on the fixed TERMINAL_GROUND, pre-rendered glow sprites, quantized-alpha tables, a 64-slot particle pool, entrance choreography and idle drift. Workflow graphs use a different substrate — React Flow (@xyflow/react 12) + ELK with the DOM NodeCard (224×128, light page ground, zoom detail bands per PRD §8.5). ActiveGraphCanvas.tsx already ported the mesh craft to CSS (breathing halo keyframes, one-shot pulse rings, motion gating), so a shared 'Culture node' that looks like the mesh nodes and lives on React Flow is a port, not a rewrite.

Graphs are visible in exactly three places: the run page (routes/RunView.tsx, Graph/Timeline toggle), the Active Graphs sub-tab (ActiveGraphCanvas, only workflows pinned by a non-terminal run per domain/active-presence.ts), and the authoring preview once source parses. The 'Node Graphs' sub-tab of /graphs is misnamed: NodeGraphsPanel renders one workflow-card per workflow_key (versions table + recent runs list) and never a graph; the 'Nodes' sub-tab renders node-definition cards. That is why a published-but-idle workflow has no graph anywhere.

Authoring is text-first by design: routes/AuthorWorkflow.tsx is a textarea + Upload… + Load a sample + Validate + Publish, its React Flow preview is explicitly read-only ('nothing opens on click') and every Handle in WorkflowNode.tsx is isConnectable={false}. The canvas library is not the gap — React Flow 12 supports drag, connect and selection natively; what is missing is the reverse direction (graph → IR → canonical JSON/YAML), per-kind property editing, and on-canvas compiler diagnostics (PRD Phase 3 names 'compiler diagnostics on canvas'). Generate (routes/GenerateWorkflow.tsx) is a separate page that asks an actor to propose source and never publishes.

claims.text: Challenge finding (data-flow lens): the workflow digest is computed over the normalized IR encoded as canonical JSON (internal/compiler/doc.go "Determinism"), and POST /v1alpha1/workflows publish is idempotent by digest — a repeat publish returns 200 with the EXISTING version (internal/api/workflows.go ~L101). Therefore a canvas edit that changes only comments, blank lines, key order or formatting has the same digest and publishes to the existing version, whose stored source is the ORIGINAL text. "Comments survive Publish" (c28/h10) is true for the file the author keeps and false for what the control plane stores, unless the version model changes.

honesty_conditions.text: A server test publishes source A, then A with only a comment changed, and asserts the second publish returns 200 with the FIRST version's stored source — documenting the fact q4 decides on.

claims.text: Challenge finding (adjacent-systems lens): WorkflowVersion already carries source, source_format, normalized_ir and digest (api/openapi/openapi.yaml WorkflowVersion). The Design gallery draws its graph from normalized_ir and offers "Open in canvas", which loads that version's stored source verbatim into the editor — so a published version's hand-written text, not a re-serialization, is what round-trips.

honesty_conditions.text: Opening a published version in the canvas shows a source pane byte-identical to the stored source; the gallery graph and the canvas graph for the same digest have identical node and edge sets.

claims.text: Challenge finding (concurrency lens), reconciled with the sweep's 0.47.19 amendment of c2: the one app-wide EventSource is opened by SharedEventsProvider at app start on any route (web/src/main.tsx, hooks/useSharedEvents.tsx) and must never reconnect (c48/h41 of the operate-through-the-ui spec), so "the Mesh connects with ?from=latest" cannot mean a second connection. The shared manager itself opens with ?from=latest, stores the stream.snapshot marker id and exposes it; a view that mounts later reads the stored marker as its boundary and fetches REST state after subscribing; every view buffers streamed events until its REST response lands and applies them idempotently by id. The cursor-less server default stays unchanged for other clients — only the web client uses the cross-run stream today (culture_nodes/cli/_commands/run.py uses the per-run stream).

honesty_conditions.text: A web test mounts the Mesh after the shared stream has been open for a while, commits a run.created between the Mesh's REST fetch and its subscription, and asserts the run is shown exactly once; a lint guard asserts exactly one EventSource construction site in web/src; the CLI test suite is unchanged.

claims.text: Challenge finding (overlooked-actors lens): `nodes worker` is its own process (cmd/nodes/worker.go; `nodes all` runs serve + scheduler + worker in-process) that holds the NODES_ACTOR_* tokens and reaches control-plane state through Postgres leases and signed callbacks, not through a registration HTTP call. So the "self-report on its poll heartbeat" (c19/c23) is a new worker-presence TABLE the worker loop writes (worker_id, hostname it reports for itself, control-plane revision, configured actor-key names, last_seen) and the API reads — a migration, which is a c19 escalation signal — and one host may run several worker processes.

honesty_conditions.text: The presence table migration is additive (no existing row rewritten), `nodes worker` writes it on every poll, `nodes all` writes it from its in-process worker, a worker test asserts a row appears within one poll interval of start, rows older than three poll intervals render as stale, and two workers on one host render as two worker nodes under one machine.

claims.text: Challenge finding (reversibility lens): web assets are embedded in the control-plane binary (webassets_embed.go), so each wave ships and rolls back as one image on thor (deploy/prod/deploy.sh); the SSE tail-only mode, the mesh endpoint and the UI that needs them are one deploy unit. The canvas adds NO new write route: Publish uses the same POST /v1alpha1/workflows and the same role gate as the text authoring page, so removing the canvas route is a pure UI rollback.

honesty_conditions.text: No new mutating route appears in api/openapi/openapi.yaml for the canvas; an e2e proves a viewer-role principal gets the same refusal from the canvas Publish as from the text page.

claims.text: Challenge finding (failure-mode / observability lens): GET /v1alpha1/actors is already "the heaviest read in the API" because it fans out (internal/api/dialinpresence.go), so the mesh endpoint must never probe bridges inside a request. A collector runs on a timer with a per-probe timeout and bounded concurrency, caches each machine fact with observed_at and the probe's error text, and the endpoint reads the cache; the mesh renders the age of every machine fact and logs each probe failure with its target.

honesty_conditions.text: A test with a bridge that never answers shows GET /mesh returning within its normal latency with that machine marked unknown and its error text; every machine fact in the payload carries observed_at; a metric or log line counts probe failures per target.

obligations.behavior: first frame is stream.snapshot with the max id; nothing at or before it streams; a run.created between marker and GET /runs is delivered exactly once
obligations.source_text: Mesh stops replaying history on arrival: web/src/hooks/useSharedEvents.tsx connects with no cursor on every page load, and internal/api/events.go's handleStreamEvents treats an absent Last-Event-ID/from as 'from the beginning of this namespace's event log', admitting every historical run.created/run.completed lifecycle event; routes/Mesh.tsx turns each into a run-added placeholder then a 3.4s linger-and-remove, so the whole run history animates through the mesh at speed. The fix is a server-side tail-only connect, ordered stream-first so the two reads have a defined boundary: the Mesh opens the stream in an explicit tail-only mode, the server's first frame is a snapshot marker naming the event-log high-water mark it will stream after, and only then does the Mesh load active runs from GET /runs, buffering every streamed event until that response lands and applying it on top keyed by run id. Reading the marker before the snapshot query makes that boundary at-least-once rather than at-most-once, which is what the data allows: GET /runs returns a pagination cursor over runs and can never carry the event log's ULID high-water mark, so no single call can hand back both atomically, and a transition committed between the two reads must therefore appear in both and reconcile, never fall between them. A Go change plus a client cursor-and-reconcile rule.

obligations.behavior: machines keyed on the bridge's self-reported preflight.host.hostname; a bridge that never answers marks its machine unknown with error text within normal latency
obligations.source_text: The Mesh is rebuilt as a React Flow + ELK graph on the terminal ground with typed nodes — machine, control plane, bridge/actor, published workflow, active run — and edges drawn only from records: actor→machine keyed on the hostname each bridge reports for ITSELF under capabilities.preflight.host.hostname (preflight.Surface's host block, which checkHost already refuses empty, and which the package doc pins as a fact only the party that can measure it may supply), run→actor (node-run attribution), run→workflow (workflow_digest), actor→workflow-node (the IR's uses refs), plus per-machine revision, install_mode, dirty flag, actor-key configuration and liveness from issue #226's surfaces; committed events still pulse one-to-one along the relevant edge; hover/keyboard inspection and the #agent-state mirror stay. No machine is derived from endpoint_ref: that column is nullable caller-supplied address text on an immutable actor revision, it goes stale on every superseded revision, migrations/pending/0036 drops it after the dial-in cutover, and a dial-in bridge has no address to read — so an actor whose surface reports no hostname is drawn as an unattributed actor rather than joined to a machine invented from an address.

obligations.behavior: presence rows carry actor-key NAMES only; a token-looking value is rejected; hostname from NODES_HOSTNAME
obligations.source_text: Machine facts on the mesh come only from surfaces that already exist or that this cycle adds to the control plane: GET /v1alpha1/version, each bridge's /v1/capabilities deployment block (package, install_mode, revision, revision_is_dirty), actor rows, and a worker/bridge self-report of configured actor-key NAMES on its poll heartbeat — never secret values, never a shell probe of a host from the control plane. Deployment-checkout HEAD/dirty state needs host access the control plane does not have and is a follow-up unless a reporting path exists.
